title: A CITY WAS STARVING SO BADLY THAT PEOPLE WERE PAYING FORTUNES FOR ALMOST NOTHING. THEN ELISHA MADE AN IMPOSSIBLE PREDICTION.
paragraphs: A CITY WAS STARVING SO BADLY THAT PEOPLE WERE PAYING FORTUNES FOR ALMOST NOTHING. THEN ELISHA MADE AN IMPOSSIBLE PREDICTION.

The Siege of Samaria became so horrific that a donkey’s head cost eighty pieces of silver and mothers were discussing the unthinkable. Then, while everyone could see only death, Elisha said that by this time tomorrow food would be abundant—and four dying outcasts were about to discover that God had already moved.
There are Bible stories we make safe because we have heard them too many times.
We know the ending.
We know God wins.
We know deliverance comes.
So we read quickly.
But imagine reading 2 Kings 6 without knowing chapter 7 exists.
Imagine being inside Samaria.
Not reading about the famine.
Smelling it.
Living it.
Watching another day begin while wondering what can possibly be sold because nearly everything worth eating has already disappeared.
This wasn't someone complaining that groceries had become expensive.
This was societal collapse.
Ben-hadad, king of Aram, had surrounded Samaria. The siege was doing exactly what ancient sieges were designed to do: isolate a population until hunger accomplished what weapons had not.
Nobody needed to storm the walls if starvation could break the people inside them.
And Scripture does not sanitize what happened.
The Hebrew says:
“וַיְהִי רָעָב גָּדוֹל בְּשֹׁמְרוֹן”
Vayehi ra'av gadol b'Shomron.
“There was a great famine in Samaria.”
Great famine.
Not inconvenience.
Not scarcity that could be solved by cutting expenses.
Famine.
Then the writer gives us prices.

A donkey's head was selling for eighty pieces of silver, while a quarter-kab of something the Hebrew text calls ḥiryônim—traditionally rendered “dove's dung,” though the precise identification has been debated—was selling for five pieces of silver.
Whatever precisely that second commodity was, the narrator's point is unmistakable.
Desperation had rewritten the economy.
Things nobody would normally value had become costly because people were starving.
And there is something frighteningly human about that.
When you become desperate enough, you can start paying enormous prices for things that cannot truly feed you.
Some people do it with money.
Some with relationships.
Some with pornography.
Some with attention.
Some with alcohol.
Some with applause.
Some with achievement.
Some with religious performance.
Some spend years purchasing tiny moments of validation with pieces of their soul.
A little affection.
A little escape.
A little pleasure.
A little numbness.
A little feeling that somebody finally sees them.
And the price keeps rising.
Your peace.
Your marriage.
Your integrity.
Your prayer life.
Your ability to look yourself in the mirror without remembering what you have been hiding.
That is one of sin's cruelest economies.
It makes almost nothing look priceless when the soul is starving.
But Samaria was about to descend somewhere darker still.
The king of Israel was walking along the city wall when a woman cried to him for help.
He asked what was wrong.
Her answer is one of those passages of Scripture you wish were not there.
But God allowed it to remain in His Word because the Bible does not pretend human brokenness is prettier than it really is.
The woman described an agreement with another mother.
They would eat her son first.
Then they would eat the other woman's son.
Her child was killed and eaten.
The next day, however, the second mother hid her own son.
Stop there.
Don't rush toward the miracle yet.
A child was dead.
A mother had participated in something almost impossible to comprehend.
Another mother was hiding her son.
A king was standing on a wall listening to the horror happening beneath his government.
This is what starvation had done.
And when the king heard it, he tore his clothes.
Underneath his royal garments, the people saw sackcloth.
He was grieving.
But grief is not necessarily repentance.
A person can hate the consequences of a broken world without surrendering the heart to God.
The king's next reaction exposes something terribly familiar.
He wanted Elisha dead.
The prophet became the target.
When people cannot control their circumstances, they often search for somebody to blame.
Sometimes even God.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
You prayed.
Nothing changed.
You waited.
Nothing moved.
You tried to obey.
The door remained closed.
You watched someone else receive the thing you begged God for.
Then a dangerous sentence quietly formed somewhere inside you:
“Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?”
That is essentially where the chapter leaves us.
And perhaps that sentence is closer to your heart than you want anyone to know.
Why should I keep praying?
Why keep believing?
Why remain faithful?
Why keep forgiving?
Why keep fighting temptation?
Why keep worshiping when heaven feels silent?
Why should I wait any longer?
Then Elisha speaks.
Not motivational optimism.
Not positive thinking.
Not a prediction based upon military intelligence.
The Hebrew begins:
“שִׁמְעוּ דְּבַר־יְהוָה”
Shim'u devar-YHWH.
“Hear the word of the LORD.”
Then comes the impossible announcement:
“כָּעֵת מָחָר”
Ka'et machar.
“About this time tomorrow…”
Tomorrow.
Elisha declares that fine flour will sell for a shekel and two measures of barley for a shekel at the gate of Samaria.
Think about the absurdity of that statement from inside the city.
Today people are paying fortunes for almost nothing.
Tomorrow flour will be affordable.
Today starvation.
Tomorrow abundance.
Today mothers are desperate.
Tomorrow food will flood the market.
And Elisha doesn't announce a five-year agricultural recovery program.
He says tomorrow.
One of the king's officers hears this and essentially responds:
Even if the LORD opened windows in heaven, could that happen?
You can almost understand his skepticism.
Almost.
Because everything visible contradicted the promise.
There was still an army outside.
Still famine inside.
Still no supply route.
Still no visible rescue force.
Still no logical mechanism connecting “today” with Elisha's “tomorrow.”
And this is where faith is often misunderstood.
Biblical faith is not pretending circumstances aren't real.
Samaria's famine was real.
The enemy was real.
The dead child was real.
The empty stomachs were real.
Biblical faith does not require you to call darkness light.
Faith takes God seriously even when you cannot yet see how His word could possibly be fulfilled.
The officer's tragedy wasn't that he understood the impossibility.
Everyone understood the impossibility.
His tragedy was treating God's power as though it were imprisoned inside the boundaries of what he could imagine.
Elisha answered that he would see the promised abundance with his own eyes...
but he would not eat from it.
Then the camera of Scripture moves.
Away from the palace.
Away from the king.
Away from Elisha.
Away from the powerful.
Toward four men sitting outside the gate.
Four men described by the text as מְצֹרָעִים — metzora'im, people afflicted with a serious skin condition that left them marginalized from ordinary community life.
They are trapped between two kinds of death.
Behind them is a starving city.
Ahead of them is an enemy army.
So they ask one of the most brutally logical questions in Scripture:
“מָה אֲנַחְנוּ יֹשְׁבִים פֹּה עַד־מָתְנוּ”
Mah anachnu yoshvim poh ad-matnu?
“Why are we sitting here until we die?”
Read that again.
Why are we sitting here until we die?
There are moments when those words stop being ancient history.
Why am I sitting in the same secret sin until something in me dies?
Why am I sitting in bitterness?
Why am I sitting in shame?
Why am I sitting behind excuses?
Why am I sitting inside a version of Christianity that knows church language but has lost hunger for Christ?
Why am I sitting here until I die?
The four men reasoned that remaining where they were meant death.
Returning to the city meant death.
Approaching the Arameans might mean death.
But there was at least the possibility of mercy.
So at twilight they got up.
No army marched with them.
No sword-bearing battalion followed.
Four desperate outcasts simply started walking.
And while they walked...
God was doing something they could not hear.
Scripture says the Lord caused the Aramean army to hear the sound of chariots, horses and a great army.
The Syrians concluded that Israel had hired foreign kings against them.
Panic erupted.
They ran.
They abandoned tents.
Horses.
Donkeys.
Food.
Silver.
Gold.
Clothing.
Everything.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
The four men did not defeat the army.
Elisha did not defeat the army.
The king did not defeat the army.
Samaria's starving population did not defeat the army.
The Lord acted.
By the time the four men reached the enemy camp, the battle they feared was effectively already over.
They arrived expecting perhaps to beg for their lives.
Instead...
silence.
An abandoned camp.
Food waiting inside tents.
Can you imagine the first bite?
Men who had been waiting to die suddenly eating food left behind by the army they feared.
Then another bite.
Then drinking.
Then discovering silver.
Gold.
Clothing.
They ate.
They drank.
They carried valuables away and hid them.
Then they returned and gathered more.
You can hardly blame them.
People who have lived with scarcity often grab tightly when abundance finally arrives.
But eventually conscience interrupted appetite.
They looked at one another.
And what they said may be the spiritual heartbeat of the entire story:
“הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה יוֹם־בְּשֹׂרָה הוּא”
Hayom hazeh yom-besorah hu.
“This day is a day of good news.”
The Hebrew word besorah means good news, glad tidings.
And they realized something.
Good news this important could not remain hidden inside their private feast.
People were starving behind those walls.
Children were starving.
Families were starving.
The city didn't know what these four men knew.
The food already existed.
The enemy had already fled.
Deliverance had already happened outside the walls.
But inside Samaria people were still behaving as though nothing had changed because they had not yet heard the news.
That image reaches far beyond Samaria.

We should be careful not to flatten this Old Testament event into an allegory in which every character secretly represents something else. Second Kings 7 is first a real account of God's deliverance of Samaria and the fulfillment of His word through Elisha.
But when Christians read this story within the whole testimony of Scripture, we cannot miss the resonance.
There is good news that cannot rightly be hoarded.
The New Testament calls it the Gospel.
And unlike Samaria's temporary rescue from famine, the Gospel addresses humanity's deepest catastrophe: sin, guilt, judgment, alienation from God and death.
The Gospel is not:
“Become better and maybe God will love you.”
It is not:
“Fix yourself before approaching Jesus.”
It is not:
“Hide the scandalous chapters and present God with the respectable version of yourself.”
The Gospel announces what God has done in Jesus Christ.
We sinned.
Christ came.
The Son of God took on flesh.
He lived without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin's judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day He rose.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our circumstances.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
At the cross, grace did not pretend sin was inexpensive.
Grace revealed exactly how costly our redemption was.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ reigning.
And now forgiveness is proclaimed to sinners who could never purchase it.
That is why grace is so scandalous.
Because the people receiving it cannot brag that they deserved it.
The four starving men didn't manufacture the feast.
They discovered it.
And sinners do not manufacture salvation.
Christ accomplished what we could not accomplish.
Salvation is received by grace through faith, and genuine faith turns us toward Christ in repentance, surrender and a transformed life.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody reading this needs.
You have spent years believing your worst chapter disqualified you from coming home.
You think Jesus would receive the cleaner version of you.
The sober version.
The sexually pure version.
The less angry version.
The version who finally has prayer figured out.
The version who stopped failing.
So you keep waiting to become worthy of grace before asking for grace.
But if you could make yourself worthy of the cross, you would not need the cross.
Jesus did not die for imaginary people with imaginary sins.
He died for sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with secrets.
People who knew better and did it anyway.
People who promised God, “Never again,” and returned.
People whose shame has been whispering:
Stay outside.
Hide.
God is tired of you.
But Scripture's answer is not that sin doesn't matter.
It matters so much that Christ died.
And Scripture's answer is not that repentance doesn't matter.
Jesus calls us to repent and believe.
The answer is that your sin does not possess greater saving power than the blood of Christ.
You are not being invited to excuse your darkness.
You are being invited to bring it into the light.
Repentance says:
No more hiding.
No more renaming sin so I can keep it.
No more pretending I can save myself.
Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.
Forgive me.
Cleanse me.
Rule me.
Change me.
I am Yours.
And maybe right now you feel like one of those four men outside Samaria.
Too broken for one world.
Terrified of the next step.
Unsure what will happen if you move toward God.
Then hear their question again:
“Why are we sitting here until we die?”
You do not need to know every detail of tomorrow before taking the next obedient step today.
Come to Christ.
Not because tomorrow will necessarily bring money.
Not because Christianity guarantees that every sickness disappears overnight.
Not because following Jesus means your enemies will always vanish before breakfast.
Second Kings 7 is not a blank cheque promising every believer a twenty-four-hour reversal of every crisis.
That would misuse the text.
Come because Jesus Christ is worthy.
Come because sin cannot give you what it promises.
Come because forgiveness is real.
Come because there is mercy for the repentant sinner.
Come because the tomb is empty.
Come because the King who knows the worst thing about you still calls sinners to Himself.
And once you have tasted the good news...
don't hide it.
That is where those four men became more than survivors.
They became messengers.
“We are not doing right,” they realized.
“This day is a day of good news, and we are keeping silent.”
There are people on your Facebook friends list who may never tell you they are starving spiritually.
The smiling profile picture won't tell you.
The family photo won't tell you.
The jokes won't tell you.
The promotion announcement won't tell you.
Somebody can look successful and still go to bed asking whether life is worth continuing.
Someone can quote Scripture publicly while privately losing the battle against temptation.
Someone can sit in church every Sunday while quietly wondering whether God could ever forgive what nobody else knows.
Someone you know may be one Gospel conversation away from discovering that Jesus has not stopped calling them.
So if this article reminded you of somebody, don't merely think about them.
Send it privately if public tagging would embarrass them.
We cannot manipulate God with engagement.
But if you genuinely want your online presence to glorify God, one practical way to do that is to use the reach He has given you to make Christ known.
Let your profile carry something besides arguments, entertainment and photographs.
Let somebody encounter the Gospel there.
You don't know who is reading quietly.
You don't know who is starving behind a screen.
You don't know whose “Samaria” is collapsing tonight.
And if this exposed something hidden in your own heart, be honest.
And if Christ has already brought you through something you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did.
Your testimony does not make you the hero.
Jesus is the Hero.
That is precisely why your testimony matters.
Because there may come a night when God's promises feel less believable than your circumstances, and you may need to remember Samaria.
At sunset, nothing looked different.
The walls still stood.
The famine still hurt.
The people still believed the enemy was outside.
Yet beyond their sight, God had already acted.
Again, this does not mean every unanswered prayer has a miracle scheduled for tomorrow.
It means visible circumstances are never the final measurement of God's sovereignty.
Elisha said, “Tomorrow.”
The officer laughed at the impossibility.
And tomorrow came.
The people eventually went out.
The abandoned camp was plundered.
Food flooded Samaria.
The prices fell exactly as the word of the LORD had declared.
And the officer who had mocked God's word saw the abundance...
but never ate it.
He was trampled at the gate.
It is a sobering ending.
Because it is possible to stand close to the evidence of God's work and remain personally untouched by its blessing.
It is possible to know Bible verses without trusting the God who spoke them.
To attend church without surrendering to Christ.
To admire Jesus without following Jesus.
To discuss grace without receiving grace.
To see bread and remain hungry.
Do not settle for proximity to Christianity.
Come to Christ Himself.
The goal isn't simply another follower.
The goal is another person repeatedly brought within reach of Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing and discipleship centered upon Jesus Christ.
It doesn't.
Not because financial support earns favor with Christ.
It cannot.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, sharing Scripture and developing resources intended to point people toward Jesus.
Not out of guilt.
Out of mission.
The four starving men eventually understood that abundance carried responsibility.
“This day is a day of good news, and we are keeping silent.”
Christians have infinitely greater news.
The Son of God came.
The cross happened.
The debt was paid.
The grave was opened.
Jesus Christ is risen.
Forgiveness is offered.
Sinners can come home.
Captives can be freed.
The ashamed can step into the light.
The spiritually starving can discover the Bread of Life.
So how could we feast on grace and never tell the hungry where the Bread is?
Maybe you entered this article feeling surrounded.
Maybe your finances look surrounded.
Your family.
Your marriage.
Your mind.
Your faith.
Maybe you have been sitting between two terrible options thinking there is no road forward.
Samaria reminds us that God does not need visible possibilities before He can act.
But the greater Gospel reminds us of something even better:
Our deepest hope is not that every earthly siege ends tomorrow.
Our hope has a name.
Jesus.
And when Jesus takes hold of a ruined story, He does not merely edit the embarrassing sentences.
He redeems the person inside them.
Peter had denial.
Paul had persecution and blood on his résumé.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Yet grace met sinners where human pride would have expected rejection.
That doesn't make sin beautiful.
It makes the Savior beautiful.
This is what we mean when we say:
From scandal...
to grace.
The scandal is real.
The wounds are real.
The consequences can be real.
Repentance is necessary.
But Jesus is greater than the chapter you thought would become your identity.
Your failure does not have to write the final sentence.
Your addiction does not have to write the final sentence.
Your shame does not have to write the final sentence.
Your past does not have to write the final sentence.
Your worst night does not have to write the final sentence.
Jesus Christ holds the pen of redemption.
So come out of hiding.
Tell the truth.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive His mercy.
Follow Him.
And when you discover the good news...
don't bury it in the tent.
Tell somebody.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is still sitting outside the gate believing death is the only ending available.
And maybe God will use the good news you refused to keep to yourself to show them otherwise.
Never forget this: the starving men thought they were walking toward death, only to discover that God had already made a way where they could see none.
